title: Date, text and publication
short: Written about 1861 (Fr260, J288) and first printed in 1891, after Dickinson's death, in an edited text that changes two key words.
body: Dickinson left the poem in a fascicle of about 1861; it was published in Poems, Second Series (1891), edited by T. W. Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd, and the archive reproduces that text. The editors regularised her dashes and punctuation and altered two words: where the archive reads 'banish us', Franklin's manuscript-based text has 'advertise', and the final stanza's 'the livelong day' replaces 'the livelong June'. Students quoting the poem should know which version they are using. The opening exclamation, with its sudden direct question to the reader, is typical of Dickinson's conversational openings: the reader is drawn into complicity before the poem has properly begun.

title: nobody / somebody
short: To be 'nobody' is to be obscure, unpublished and unknown; the poem turns social insignificance into a privilege.
body: 'Somebody' and 'nobody' were everyday words for persons of importance and of none (OED). The speaker claims nobody-hood as a secret club of two. Classically minded readers have heard a faint echo of Odysseus, who tells the Cyclops his name is 'Nobody' (Outis) and escapes by that anonymity (Odyssey 9.366-67); the echo is unprovable but apt, since here too namelessness is a form of protection. Biographically, the poem is often linked to Dickinson's refusal to seek publication, though it dates from before her correspondence with Higginson began in April 1862, and it should not be read only as autobiography.

title: 'a pair of us -- don't tell!'
short: The reader is recruited into a conspiracy of two nobodies, who must keep their nobody-hood secret.
body: The joke is that being nobody, which ought to be nothing, becomes a secret worth keeping: if the two were discovered, they would lose their anonymity. The hushed 'don't tell!' gives the poem the tone of children whispering, and the conspiratorial pair is the opposite of the public 'somebody' with an audience of a whole bog. Dickinson's poems often address an unnamed 'you' whose identity remains open: here it is any reader willing to admit to obscurity.

title: 'They 'd banish us' (manuscript 'advertise')
short: The 1891 editors printed 'banish'; Dickinson wrote 'advertise'. The two words make opposite jokes.
body: In Franklin's text the somebodies would 'advertise' the pair: publicise them, and so destroy their precious nobody-hood by making them somebodies. That is the sharper paradox, since the threat is fame, and it fits the second stanza's satire on publicity. The editors' 'banish' makes the threat exclusion, a more conventional idea of the unconventional pair as outcasts. Most modern editors and critics follow the manuscript, and the change is a standard example of how the early editions normalised Dickinson's wit. 'Advertise' in Webster's 1844 sense also meant simply to inform or make known.

title: 'How dreary to be somebody!'
short: The second stanza inverts expectation: celebrity, not obscurity, is dreary.
body: The adjective 'dreary' is usually attached to loneliness; here it describes fame. The stanza is a satire on public life: politicians, lecturers and, by implication, published poets who must constantly tell their name. Dickinson's America was a culture of the lyceum lecture, the stump speech and the newspaper, and Amherst itself was a political town (her father, Edward Dickinson, served in Congress in 1853-55). 'How public' makes publicity a kind of indecency.

title: like a frog
short: The celebrity croaks his own name all day long, as a frog repeats its single call.
body: The comic simile reduces the 'somebody' to a frog whose only song is its own name, endlessly repeated. Frog-calls were proverbially monotonous, and the frog who puffs himself up is also a fable figure of vanity (Aesop's frog who swells to rival an ox). The joke depends on the sound: the frog's croak is a self-advertisement that only a bog could admire.

title: the livelong day (manuscript 'June')
short: 'Livelong' means the whole length of; Dickinson wrote 'the livelong June', which the 1891 editors made 'day'.
body: 'Livelong' (from 'lief' + 'long', dear and long) is an intensive used of time felt as tediously long (OED). 'The livelong day' is a stock phrase; Dickinson's 'the livelong June' is fresher and more exact, since June is the season when frogs call loudest, and it makes the self-advertisement last a whole month rather than a day. As with 'banish', the editors replaced a surprising word with an expected one.

title: an admiring bog
short: The audience of the famous is a swamp: wet, stagnant and indiscriminate in its admiration.
body: The poem's final rhyme 'frog / bog' clinches the satire: the public that admires celebrity is itself a mire, and the frog is exactly the kind of somebody such a bog would admire. 'Admiring' here keeps its older sense of 'wondering at' as well as approving. The form, two quatrains in loose common metre with an exclamatory, almost nursery-rhyme lightness, makes the attack seem playful; its target, the reputation economy of public life, is serious.
